title: Operational semver policy for runtime: compatibility vectors, LTS channels, rollout gates & upgrade tooling
creator: Maya Chen
description:
Summary: This ticket captures the operational semantic versioning (semver) rules, LTS channel lifecycle, rollout gating requirements, and the supporting upgrade/tooling guidelines for Redwood's serving runtime. Goal is to provide deterministic rules engineers can follow when proposing API/runtime changes so we can: (1) avoid accidental breaking changes in hosted and Dedicated deployments, (2) provide predictable upgrade windows for Private customers, and (3) enable automated checks and migration helpers in CI and the release tooling.

Scope: Applies to the serving runtime binary and control-plane API surfaces used by customers: HTTP/RPC public APIs, client SDK wire contracts, model artifact layout and serialization (checkpoint/kvcache), runtime plugin/hook interfaces, and on-disk metadata formats. This policy does NOT change semantic versioning for ephemeral developer tools (local dev CLI) unless they are shipped with the runtime images.

Versioning rules:
- Core format: MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH (optional pre-release tags).
- MAJOR: increments for incompatible changes across any compatibility vector. A MAJOR bump requires a migration path, release notes with migration steps, and a deprecation timeline enforced in the release process.
- MINOR: new backward-compatible functionality, new endpoints or features that do not change existing request/response semantics or on-disk formats. MINOR releases may introduce opt-in preview flags for features that will be enabled by default in a future MINOR/MAJOR.
- PATCH: bug fixes and behavior-preserving performance improvements; must not modify public contracts.

Compatibility vectors (explicit):
1) Public API contract (HTTP/gRPC endpoints, schema shapes).
2) Client SDK behavior (request/response semanatics, retry semantics).
3) Model artifact/serialization (checkpoint directory layout, tensor dtype/ordering, KV cache format).
4) Runtime on-disk metadata and upgrade markers.
5) Runtime plugin/hook ABI (loading symbols, hook signatures).

Compatibility levels: engineers must mark changed surfaces as one of: stable | tolerated | breaking.
- stable: guaranteed compatibility between MINOR releases; only PATCH allowed for fixes.
- tolerated: allowed to change in MINOR with opt-in flags and deprecation notices; 1 MINOR release grace period for clients to opt in/out.
- breaking: require MAJOR and full migration support.

Deprecation policy:
- When a surface is to be removed or changed incompatibly, add a deprecation notice in the next MINOR release notes and include: guide, example flags, migration steps, and an opt-out config flag where feasible.
- Minimum deprecation window: 3 MINOR releases or 12 months (whichever is longer) before removing a deprecated surface in a MAJOR release.
- Runtime provides runtime.legacy.enable_* flags to keep deprecated semantics for the configured lifecycle; flags may be removed only in a MAJOR release.

Rollout gates and automation:
- All releases targeting hosted or dedicated fleets must pass the automated gating flow before wide rollout:
  * CI compatibility-check (see tooling below) must emit a compatibility report with no 'breaking' findings or must list explicit acceptance by Release Manager.
  * Canary rollout: 0 -> 1% -> 10% -> 50% -> 100% by traffic with at least 24h between major steps unless accelerated by Release Manager.
  * Health gates: SLOs (error rate, p50/p95 latency) and error budget burn evaluated at each step. Auto-rollback triggers if: error budget burn > 30% in 1h window or spike in unhandled exceptions > 3x baseline.
  * Observability must surface per-route token cost and tail latency regressions; any >15% regression in token cost requires explicit product approval.
- Private deployments: release artifacts will be published and marked with LTS tags; customers are given migration notes and compatibility reports. Private/fleet owners may opt into Hosted-like canary using redwood-upgrade tooling in their environment.

LTS channel policy:
- LTS cadence: new LTS snapshot every 6 months (approx). Each LTS is supported for 18 months from initial publish.
- Only MAJOR and MINOR patches that do not change declared compatibility vectors will be backported to LTS; security and critical fixes (high severity) get expedited patches.
- LTS channels are named lts-Y.M (example: lts-2.6). LTS images include a compatibility manifest describing supported client SDK versions and retained legacy flags.

Upgrade tooling and CI integration: "redwood-upgrade" (CLI) and the compatibility-checker library are required components. Requirements: 
- redwood-upgrade check: analyzes a target runtime image against a baseline image and emits a machine-readable compatibility-report (JSON) and a human summary. This runs in PR CI for runtime changes.
- redwood-upgrade plan: generates a step-by-step upgrade plan for Dedicated and Private customers including migration commands for on-disk metadata and KV cache rewriters.
- redwood-upgrade apply: orchestrates safe upgrade steps for Dedicated pools (drain, warm cache, apply new image, smoke test, promote).
- redwood-upgrade dry-run/rollback: supports dry-run and rollback with snapshot restore for on-prem deployments.
- Compatibility-checker: library used in unit/integ tests to assert no unintended schema/wire changes. All runtime PRs must include a compatibility-checker pass or an explicit justification and Release Manager override.

Governance and process:
- Change author responsibilities: 1) add an explicit compatibility statement in the PR description (vector-by-vector), 2) run redwood-upgrade check and attach report, 3) include migration steps if any.
- API Freeze: 2 weeks before GA release, no non-trivial breaking changes accepted.
- Release Manager responsibilities: sign-off on compatibility report, approve opt-in previews, schedule canary windows, trigger auto-rollbacks when gates fail.
- Security review required when changes affect auth, telemetry, audit trail, or on-disk encryption flags.

Examples (rule-of-thumb):
- Adding a new optional field to a response -> MINOR with no opt-in needed (stable).
- Changing a required field name in response -> MAJOR (breaking).
- Reordering internal on-disk checkpoint shards (visible to users) -> MINOR if old format supported with migration; MAJOR if old format dropped.
- Changing client retry semantics -> MINOR if backward-compatible; MAJOR if changes invalidate idempotency guarantees.

Release checklist (PR author):
- [ ] Update CHANGELOG entry describing compatibility impact and migration steps.
- [ ] Attach compatibility-report.json from redwood-upgrade check.
- [ ] Add deprecation notice and legacy flag when removing behaviour.
- [ ] Run smoke/integration tests against a baseline image.
- [ ] Add e2e scenario showing TL tests for SLOs.

Release checklist (Release Manager):
- [ ] Confirm compatibility report and PR statement.
- [ ] Approve canary plan and windows.
- [ ] Ensure monitoring dashboards are configured for the rollout.
- [ ] Verify security review if flagged.

Open tasks / next steps:
1) Implement the compatibility-report schema and add a redwood-upgrade CI job template (owner: Eng - infra).
2) Wire compatibility-checker into runtime unit and integration tests.
3) Build release-manager dashboard that summarizes compatibility findings and gate state.
4) Draft customer-facing migration playbook for Private customers (docs owner: Solutions).

- Prototype tool: https://github.com/redwood-inference/redwood-upgrade (prototype branch: compat-checker)
